edges.effect_quant: The green-tea-specific meta-analysis reported lower endometrial-cancer risk, but the broader updated tea literature was neutral overall.
edges.mechanism: Green-tea catechins may influence endometrial carcinogenesis through insulin signaling, inflammation, and estrogen-related pathways rather than through one dominant anticancer mechanism. That gives the signal biologic plausibility, but it also helps explain why green tea can look more promising than mixed-tea categories in pooled studies.
edges.summary: The strongest paper for this edge is the 2016 green-tea-specific meta-analysis showing lower endometrial-cancer risk at higher intake. An updated umbrella view of tea and cancer still sees gynecologic protection as plausible, but the later all-tea meta-analysis was neutral overall, so the safest call is tentative benefit with meaningful uncertainty.
edges.caveats: Several of the newer syntheses combine black and green tea, which likely dilutes any green-tea-specific effect. Confounding by regional diet patterns and tea-preparation habits also makes the true magnitude hard to pin down.
